sections.name: introduction
sections.content:
INTRODUCTION: Historically, psychiatric disor-
ders have been distinguished from neurolog-
ical disorders by the ab sence of the associated
histological pathology observed in neurological
c o n d i t i o n s .B u t ,o v e rt h ep a s t1 5y e a r s ,e p i g e -netic and transcriptional profiling of postmor-
tem brain samples from multiple psychiatric
conditions, including autism spectrum dis-
order (ASD), have revealed robust underlying
molecular differences. I nA S D ,t h i sr e f l e c t su p -
regulation of immune signaling genes, down-
regulation of neuronal markers and synaptic
genes, and a blunting of gene expression sig-natures of cortical regional identity. How a
genetically complex condition such as ASD
converges on shared transcriptional altera-
tions remains a mystery. This gap is further
amplified by the lack of biological insightsinto the differences in laminar and cell type –
specific pathways affected in ASD and the
underlying gene regulatory mechanisms.

sections.name: rationale
sections.content:
RATIONALE: We reasoned that deep molecular
profiling at the single-cell level would inform
our understanding of changes in cortical cell
types and circuits and, when integrated withgenetic risk factors, enable identification of
candidate drivers of pathways altered in ASD.
Further, knowledge of these pathways at a cel-
lular level would inform mechanistically driven
therapeutic development.
RESULTS: We conducted single-nucleus RNA
sequencing (snRNA-seq) and single-nucleus as-
say for transposase-accessible chromatin with
sequencing (snATAC-seq) in a large ASD and
control (CTL) cohort, as a core component of
the PsychENCODE Cons ortium (https://www.
psychencode.org/), to identify cell type –specific
changes and the cellular regulatory networksperturbed by genetic risk factors. Our ap-
proach (on average >10,000 cells per individual
and >1860 genes per cell) enabled identification
of all 26 major cortical cell types, validated with
published cortical cell atlases. We also identified
cell states, primarily activated forms of mi-
croglia (MG), oligodendrocytes (ODCs), as-
trocytes (ASTROs), and blood-brain barrier
cells, observed predominantly in ASD. Changes
in cell composition in ASD were subtle, involving
increases in activated mi croglia and astrocyte
states, which are very rarely observed in controls.
In contrast to the minor changes in cell
composition, the changes observed in gene
expression in ASD were substantial: 2166 down-
regulated and 1319 up-regulated genes across
35 cell types, most of which were cell type spe-
cific. Through integration of snRNA-seq, snATAC-
seq, and spatial transcriptomics, we identified
regulatory networks driving cell type –specific
transcriptional changes and their location
within cortical laminae. These analyses dem-
onstrate concentration o f activated microglia,
astrocytes, and somatostatin (SST) interneurons
in superficial cortical laminae, in conjunction
with profound down-regulation of synaptic gene
expression and up-regulation of stress-response
and proinflammatory pathways in inter- and
intrahemispheric projection neurons. A large
proportion of these changes could be ascribed to
specific transcriptional drivers, and both the driv-
ers and their targets were enriched in genes
harboring common and rare genetic risk for ASD.

sections.name: conclusion
sections.content:
CONCLUSION: These analyses refine our knowl-
edge of cellular and circuit alterations in the
brain in ASD. By identifying and validating tran-
scriptional drivers enriched in rare and common
genetic risk variants, we have discovered a link be-
tween autism genetic susceptibility and molec-
ular and cellular circuits and pathways, providing
a roadmap for understanding cellular interac-
tions and therapeutic development in ASD. ▪RESEARCH |DECODING THE BRAIN

Molecular cascades and cell type –specific signatures
in ASD revealed by single-cell genomics
Brie Wamsley1,2, Lucy Bicks2,3, Yuyan Cheng2, Riki Kawaguchi2, Diana Quintero2, Michael Margolis4,
Jennifer Grundman4, Jianyin Liu2, Shaohua Xiao2, Natalie Hawken4,
Samantha Mazariegos2, Daniel H. Geschwind1,2,3,4*
Genomic profiling in postmortem brain from autistic individuals has consistently revealed convergent
molecular changes. What drives these changes and how they relate to genetic susceptibility in this
complex condition are not well understood. We perfor med deep single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq)
to examine cell composition and transcriptomi cs, identifying dysregulation of cell type –specific gene
regulatory networks (GRNs) in autism spectrum disord er (ASD), which we corrobora ted using sing le-nucleus
assay for transposase-accessible chromatin with sequ encing (snATAC-seq) and spatial transcriptomics.
Transcriptomic changes were primarily cell type specific, involving multiple cell types, most prominently
interhemispheric and callosal-projecting neurons, interneurons within superficial laminae, and distinct
glial reactive states involving oligodendrocytes, microglia, and astrocytes. Autism-associated GRN
drivers and their targets were enriched in rare and common genetic risk variants, connecting autism
genetic susceptibility and cellular and circuit alterations in the human brain.
Psychiatric disorders are defined primar-
ily by behavioral and cognitive character-
istics and are classically distinguished
from neurological disorders by the ab-sence of the associated visible histo-
logical pathology observed in neurological
conditions. However, a growing body of evi-
dence based on genomic profiling reveals con-
sistent molecular differences in brain tissue
from specific neuropsychiatric conditions com-
pared with brain tissue from neurotypical in-
dividuals ( 1–5). In autism spectrum disorder
(ASD), robust transcriptomic and epigenetic
alterations in the cerebral cortex have been
documented over the past decade, delineating
a reproducible pattern of molecular differences
(5–13). This robust molecular signature ob-
tained primarily from transcriptomic profiling
of bulk cortical tissue has identified convergent
biological pathways in the ASD brain, which is
characterized by an up-regulation of immune
signaling genes, down-regulation of specific
neuronal markers and synaptic genes, and an
attenuation of the typical patterns of gene ex-
pression associated with cortical regional iden-
tity (6–8,12–14).
These genomic data represent an essential
lens through which to understand the cellularand physiological changes occurring in the
brains of autistic individuals and to describe
potential causal mecha nisms through their in-
tegration with genetic risk variants ( 1,4,5).
However, small sample sizes, in the case of
single-cell analysis ( 13), or profiling restricted
to bulk tissue have limited biological insights
as to the differences in laminar, circuit-level,
and cell type –specific pathways affected in
ASD, as well as their underlying gene regula-
tory mechanisms. To address these limitations,
we leveraged advances in single-cell analyses to
profile the largest ASD cohort to date, consist-
ing of 63 cases and controls, including five cases
of a monogenic cause of ASD, 15q11-13 dupli-
cation [(dup)15q11-13]. This resource, generated
as a core component of the PsychENCODE
Consortium ( 1,2,4,5,8), enabled our iden-
tification of the major cortical cell types af-
fected in the ASD cortex, including alterations
in glia cell composition and cell type –specific
transcriptional cascade s linking genes to func-
tion. Through integration of single-nucleus
RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq), single-nucleus
assay for transposase-ac cessible chromatin with
sequencing (snATAC-seq), and layer-specific spa-
tial transcriptomics, we describe and validate
regulatory networks driving cell type –specific
transcriptional changes and their location
within cortical laminae, providing a deeper
understanding of the biological mechanismsthat underlie ASD.

sections.name: results
sections.content:
Results
Single-cell genomic analysis of human ASD
and control cortex
We generated snRNA-seq from the human
frontal cortex (Brodmann areas 9 and 4/6)from 33 ASD and 30 control subjects (Fig. 1A
and table S1A), profiling, on average, >10,000
cells per individual (fig. S1, A and B). We
included five individuals with a monogen-
ic form of ASD, 15q duplication syndrome
[(dup)15q11-13; table S1A], where transcrip-
tomic changes in bulk tissue mirror those ob-
served from cases of idiopathic ASD ( 7,8).
Individual samples were taken from patients
ranging in age from 2 to 60 years (mean age:
20) and were selected to be matched by age, sex,
and cause of death balanced across cases and
controls (fig. S1, B to D, and table S1A). We
isolated >800,000 nuclei and performed snRNA-
seq using the 10x Genomics platform (Materi-
als and methods). After quality control and
doublet removal, we analy zed high-quality tran-
scriptomes from 591,043 nuclei representing
306,347 cells from ASD subjects and 284,696
cells from control subje cts (average read depth
of 6.6 × 104per cell) with a mean of 1860 genes
and 4164 RNA molecules detected per cell (fig.
S1B), which provided an increase in power over
previous work ( 13) (table S1B). We simulta-
neously isolated nuclei to generate chroma-
tin conformation states using snATAC-seq in
22 cases and controls to validate predicted cell
type –specific regulatory networks through
identification of enrich ed transcription factor
(TF) binding sites with open chromatin and
TF footprinting analyses (Fig. 1A).
We performed unsupervised clustering of
transcriptional signatures from both ASD cases
and controls while considering biological and
technical sources of variation (methods). Visual-
ization of single-nuclei transcriptomes grouped
nuclei into 35 clusters that were not driven by
batch, Brodmann area, or individual samples
(Fig. 1, B and C, and fig. S1, A, C, and D). We
annotated the clusters into seven major classes
of cortical cell types —neurons, specifically ex-
citatory neurons (Ex ne urons) and inhibitory
neurons (INTs); glial ce lls, including microglia
(MG), astrocytes (ASTRO), oligodendrocyte
progenitor cells (OPCs), and oligodendrocytes
(ODCs); and blood-brain barrier (BBB) cells —
on the basis of previousl y established cell type –
specific canonical gene sets from both human
and mouse datasets ( 15–19), revealing the ex-
pected neuronal-to-glial ratio within human
cortex ( 18) (Fig. 1D and fig. S1E). Next, we
annotated distinct subgroups within each
major class by aligning our cell clusters with
reference data from the Brain Initiative Cell
Census Network (BICCN) ( 18) and the Allen
Brain Atlas ( 19), as well as a previous snRNA-
seq dataset from individuals with ASD and
controls ( 13) and using cluster-specific dif-
ferential marker genes (table S1C; methods).
Each of our 35 clusters corresponded with the
cell profiles previously defined (Fig. 1E and table
S1D), representing twice the number of cell
clusters identified in the previous, smaller ASD
single-cell analysis ( 13). Additionally, given theDECODING THE BRAIN

larger number of cells and cohort of individuals
profiled here, we defined a number of cell types
and states not previously described in the hu-
man brain atlas ( 18,19)( F i g .1 Ea n dt a b l eS 1 ,B
and D), including ASD-specific states, which most-
ly represent BBB cells and reactive glial states.
Within non-neuronal populations, BBB sub-
types separated according to specific markers
into endothelial cells, pericytes, and smooth
muscle (SM) cell types ( 20)( F i g .1 ,Da n dE ,
and fig. S2A). Astrocytes separated into three
clusters by expression of specific markers an-
notating two gray matter or protoplasmic astro-
cyte clusters, one homeostatic (ASTRO2) ando n er e a c t i v e( A S T R O 1 ) ,a n do n ew h i t em a t t e r
astrocyte cluster (ASTRO3) ( 21) (fig. S2B). We
also generated a small spatial transcriptomics
dataset (Fig. 1A and fig. S2C; methods) with
sufficient resolution to map specific cellular
signatures onto their locations relative to cor-
tical laminae and white matter. To map these
cluster-specific signatures onto the cortical
layers, we filtered cluster marker gene sets from
the snRNA-seq data into sets of differentially
expressed genes for each cell type (methods
and table S1C). Using this strategy, we con-
firmed the known patterns of cell position in the
cortex. White matter or fibrous astrocytes were
l o c a t e di nw h i t em a t t e ra n dl a y e r1 ,w h e r e a s
reactive protoplasmic astrocytes were found
in the gray matter layers ( 22) (fig. S2D). ODC
cluster expression profiles were separated by
their maturity and myelination capabilities
(ODC1 being the most mature, and ODC3
the least mature) ( 23) (fig. S2E). OPC clusters
separated according to maturation of myeli-
nating properties and subtype, with OPCS2
expressing the most-mature myelination pro-
file, and OPCS1 being immature cells, whereas
OPCS3 were delineated by BCAS1 (brain en-
riched myelin associated protein 1) and GPR17
(G protein –coupled receptor 17), which in-
dicates that they are a specific type of OPC
that supports synaptic function ( 24,25) (fig.
S2F). MG subtypes were mainly split into two
states: one homeostatic (MG1) and the other
reactive (MG2 & BBB_MG3) , differentiated by
the expression of known markers ( 26) (fig.
S2G). Homeostatic MG1 was found primarily
within white matter a n dw a sm u c hl e s sa b u n -
dant in gray matter. MG2 distribution was very
similar to distribution of homeostatic MG1, with
greater abundance in layer 1 (fig. S2H, left and
middle panels).
Ex neuron subtypes were separated by marker
genes associated with known superficial-to-
deep cortical distribution and axonal projection
trajectories ( 27,28) (fig. S2I). For Ex neurons,
we found that, in all cases, the cluster expres-
sion profiles predict their locations within the
spatial transcriptomics data —with layer 2/3
Ex neurons ’marker gene expression located in
the superficial layers, and layer 5/6 Ex neurons ’
profiles observed most highly in deeper layers(fig. S2J). INT subtypes were annotated on the
basis of canonical marker genes and differential
gene expression associated with INT ontologies
(27–30). We defined one somato statin (SST+) clus-
ter, two parvalbumin (PV+) clusters, one vasoin-
testinal peptide cluster (VIP+) that also contained
calretinin cells (CR+), one reelin (RE+) cluster,
and another cluster that consisted of tyrosine-
protein kinase KIT (KI T+) cells and synaptic
vesicle glycoprotein 2C (SV2C+) cells (fig. S3A).
Mapping the cluster-specific profiles shows that
these INT subtypes were distributed evenly across
laminae in the spatial data, with the exception
of the caudal ganglionic eminence (CGE) –derived
cluster signature, which was less abundant in
layer 4, matching its known cortical distribu-
tions in humans ( 31) (fig. S3B).
Cell composition changes in ASD
We next performed cell composition analysis
to determine whether any cell types were re-
duced or more abundant in the ASD cortex
compared with controls (see methods). In
agreement with previous analysis ( 13,32,33),
we detected a small but significant increase in
reactive forms of microglia ( P=0 . 0 4 )a n da
similar trend in astrocytes ( P= 0.10) (Fig. 1F
and table S2, A and B). The laminar distribu-
t i o no ft h er e a c t i v eM G 2c l u s t e rs i g n a t u r ei nA S D
from the spatial transcriptomics data demon-
strated an increase in MG2 within gray matter
laminae in ASD compared with control (Fig.
1F and fig. S2H, center panel). We observed
no other significant changes in glial or neu-
ronal cell type abundance, so we next assessed
cell type –specific transcriptional changes.
Overview of the cell type –specific transcriptional
changes in ASD
We detected widespread tr anscriptional changes
encompassing most cell types; we identified

Glial changes
Glial cells in ASD were primarily characterizedby changes in the state of these cells from a
homeostatic, or resting, state to reactive or ac-
tivated inflammatory states, compared with
controls. This change was illustrated by up-
regulation of cell type –specific responses to
inflammatory and interferon signaling and a
parallel decrease in expression of homeostatic
genes ( 21,26). We describe in the following
paragraphs the ASD reactive inflammatory
states in the major glial types: astrocytes, mi-
croglia, and ODCs.
Genes up-regulated in protoplasmic (PP) gray
matter astrocytes (ASTRO1) represent astrocyte
proliferation (including FOXO3 ,RFX7 , and
ZEB1 ) and likely lie downstream of TGF- band
interferon signaling through major histocom-
patibility complex (MHC) , other neural-immune
receptors (including HLA-B ,HLA-C ,HLA-E ,
CD44 ,IFI6,IFITM2 ,IFGR1 ,TGFBR2 , and
BMP7 ), and their inflammatory response effec-
tors (including IRF1,JAK3 ,MED12L ,SMARCA2 ,
STAT1/3 ,a n d SMAD1/3 ;F i g .3 Aa n dt a b l eS 4 A )
(44,45), which are up-regulated in parallel.
Fibrous (FB) astrocytes (ASTRO3) exhibited
similar changes, such as up-regulation of MHC
and other receptors (including HLA-B ,HLA-C ,
HLA-E ,CD99 ,CD44 ,a n d NTRK2 ), but differed
by up-regulation of cytoskeleton morphogene-
sis and focal adhesion signaling (genes includ-
ingITGB5 ,ITGAV ,TAB2 ,KALRN ,a n d NAV3 ),
suggesting changes in morphology or projec-
tions from white matter FB astrocytes in the ASD
cortex. FB astrocytes (ASTRO3) also up-regulated
genes related to stress-related apoptosis and un-
folded protein response (involving
DNAJA4 ,
HSP90AA1 ,HSPA1B ,BAG3 ,a n d DAB2IP )( F i g .
3B and table S4A). Both PP and FB astrocytes
exhibited a down-regulation of lipid and cho-
lesterol biosynthesis pathway genes ( HMGCS1 ).
However, PP astrocytes had down-regulated
growth factor and NTRK signaling genes, where-
as the opposite was true for FB astrocytes in ASD
relative to controls. Spe cifically, FB astrocytes
up-regulated expression of TGF- bsignaling(TGFB1 ), growth factors ( VEGFA ), and extra-
cellular matrix proteins (including ADAM12
andADAMTS17 ) (Fig. 3B and table S4A).
Microglia (MG2) manifested an increase in
reactive-state markers, as highlighted by the
up-regulation of known prophagocytotic genes
(such as P2RX7 ,TLR1/2/5 ,a n d CD68 ), includ-
ing pronounced up-regulation of the extra-
cellular signaling molecule, SPP1 ( 46)( F i g .3 C ) .
MG2 cells also expressed a higher number of
MHC I and II class molecules, complement,
and receptors (involving HLA-A/B/C ,FCGR1A/
1B/3A ,C1QC ,C1QA ,TNR,a n d TGFBR1 ), more
so than the other glial cell classes. In ASD,reactive MG2 cells also increased expression
of genes related to cell morphogenesis (includ-
ingCAMKV ,TAOK1/3 ,CTNNB1 ,MAPK10/14 ,
andJAK2/3 ) and integrin signaling (including
CD68 ,CD86 ,ITGB1 ,ITGAX ,ITGAV ,a n d ITGA9 ),
which suggests an increase in migration and
formation of contacts with other cells (Fig. 3C
and table S4A). Since many of these changes
are thought to be downstream of cytokine sig-
naling, we hypothesize from these data that
SPP1 may be acting as an extracellular element
responsible for coor dinating the cell –cell inter-
actions putatively directing synaptic and/or
cellular removal in activated MG (
46,47).
We also observed that ODCs have shifted
from a homeostatic state to a more immuno-
reactive state in ASD, another glial change
that has not previously been recognized. For
example, oligodendrocytes in cluster ODC1
up-regulated genes related to inflammatory
and energy stress response (involving IFIT1 ,
BAG3 ,ABAT ,EARS2 ,NMNAT3 ,EIF4A1 , and
EIF3A ) and histone modifying enzymes (in-
volving HDAC4/5/7 ,KDM5A ,EP300 ,a n dKMT2A )
(Fig. 3D and table S4A). However, ODC1 also
contained a substantial number of down-
regulated genes, the largest of any glia cell
type and similar in magnitude to that of super-
ficial L23 Ex neurons (Fig. 2B). Enriched down-
regulated pathways included cadherin signaling
(including CTNNB1/2 ,GSK3B ,FZD3 ,a n d CDH2/
8/11/19/20 ), transport along microtubule (in-
cluding KIF3A andDOCK9/10/3/5 ), and mye-
lination (including MBP ,PLP1 ,MAG ,JAM3 ,
LGI4 ,a n d MYRF ), which predict a potential
reduction in the capability of ODC1 cells to ma-
ture and functionally extend their processes,
adhere, and properly myelinate neuronal axons
(Fig. 3D and table S4A).

To validate these network predictions, we
next tested whether modulating TF expressionchanged expression of regulon target genes using
publicly available experimental data from the
Connectivity Map (CMAP) Library of Integrated
Network-Based Cellular Signatures (LINCS) re-
source [ https://clue.io/data/CMap2020#LINCS2020
(52); methods], which is a database of standard-
ized experimental knockdowns with short hair-
pin RNA (shRNA) and CRISPR knockouts of
>7000 genes in multiple cell types. These analy-
ses, which permitted testing of >130 TFs to
target gene relationships of regulons, showed
significant agreement between our predicted
regulatory networks and experimental RNA-
seq knockout or knockdown of regulon TF
drivers in neural cells, providing external ex-
perimental validation of the regulon networks
(Prange = 1.76 × 10
−4to 4.86 × 10−13permu-
tation, see methods; fig. S8, A and B). We also
leveraged a published Perturb-seq dataset in
K562 cells to test 10 overlapping TFs from
both datasets [( 52); methods], which also con-
firmed that their knockouts resulted in signif-
icant changes in the predicted regulon target
genes ( P=1 . 4 5×1 0−6permutation, see meth-
ods; fig. S8C). These findings support our
regulon network relationships between TFs
and downstream genes across a range of cell
types and experimental manipulations.
snATAC-seq and TF footprinting validate
regulatory network predictions
Although SCENIC predictions have been shown
to be reliable in predicti ng experimentally val-
idated regulatory networks ( 1,53–55)a n d ,m o r e -
over, were supported by the in vitro experimental
perturbation data above, we next sought to
further validate regulatory changes of TFs. We
investigated chromatin accessibility by per-
forming snATAC-seq from a subset of the same
22 samples (12 cases and 10 controls) subjected
to scRNA-seq (methods; table S6A). We gen-
erated >100,000 single-nucleus profiles after
quality control filtering, which we integrated
with the snRNA-seq to verify and validate cell
type cluster annotations (Fig. 6A and fig. S9, A
and B; methods). We observed a high concor-
dance between the snATAC-seq and snRNA-
seq clusters, as evidenced by high correlations
between cluster expression profiles (table S6B;
methods). Moreover, we assessed the overlapbetween snATAC-seq differential chromatin
accessibility and snRNA-seq –derived gene ex-
pression changes when there were sufficient
numbers of cells and gene expression changes
for adequate power, finding significant overlap
for most cell types as expected (figs. S10, A to E,
and S11, A to E; Prange = 1.1 × 10−210to 0.04,
hypergeometric test).
We next leveraged the open chromatin pro-
files from each major cell type to assess changes
in TF binding on the basis of DNA footprinting
using TOBIAS ( 56,57) (Fig. 6B; methods). DNA
footprints overlapping with TF motifs were
defined as direct TF binding sites. TF bindingactivities were then quantified by scoring each
footprint ’s depleted signal at its predicted
binding site relative to the surrounding back-
ground chromatin accessibility (methods). Using
this approach allowed us to more accurately
recover the binding activities of hundreds of
TFs at a time in comparison to other technol-
o g i e st h a tp e r m i ta s s e s s m e n to ft h ea c t i v i t yo f
one TF at a time ( 56). We focused on TFs pre-
dicted to account for the major changes in
DEGs described above (Figs. 2 to 4 and fig. S6).
Within Ex L23 neurons, we observed that 48%
of the transcriptionally down-regulated TFs
predicted to drive downstream DEGs within
the network in ASD have changes in binding
occupancy within the relevant TF DNA foot-
prints (table S7A). For example, in EXT_6_L23
neurons, we saw a decrease in the footprint
activity of BCL6 (P=2 . 4 5×1 0
−114),TCF3 (P=
1.28 × 10−63), and MAFB (P=9 . 1 2×1 0−100)a s
well as an increase in binding for up-regulated
TFs such as FOSB (P=1 . 4 0×1 0−195),JDP2 (P=
1.24 × 10−196), and SMAD5 (P=4 . 1 6×1 0−128;
Fig. 6C) with examples of altered footprints
forMEIS3 andELK1 (Fig. 6D, footprints, and
table S7A). Likewise, within reactive MG2, we
validated the changes in target binding for
43% of transcriptionally altered TFs by foot-
printing (table S7B). We observed increases in
TF activity for IRF7 (P=2 . 3 5×1 0−132)a n d
POU2F2 (P=5 . 3 7×1 0−107)( F i g .6 Ea n dt a b l e
S7B) with examples of altered footprints for
JUND andNFKB1 (Fig. 6F) in MG2. Altogether,
we found that the SCENIC regulatory net-
works and DEGs were mostly supported by TF
occupancy changes within open chromatin in
ASD relative to controls, which, when com-
bined with the perturbation experiments (fig.
S8), provide strong orthogonal experimental
support for regulon activity changes in ASD.
ASD risk gene enrichment
To determine whether these regulons repre-sent known causal aspects of ASD biology, we
next tested whether the drivers or their down-
stream gene targets were enriched in known
ASD risk genes (SFARI syndromic, tiers 1 and
2; methods). Indeed, 30 of the regulons dys-
regulated in ASD brain were driven by high-
confidence TF risk genes from the SFARIdatabase, a significant enrichment (including
CUX1 ,CHD2 ,FOXP1 ,BCL11A ,a n d SOX5 ;f i g .
S12, rare, OR = 1.64, P= 0.004, hypergeometric
test). Further, 21 of these regulons were en-
riched for genes harboring common genetic
susceptibility for ASD ( 37) (including CELF4 ,
SREBF2 ,ETV5 ,a n d NR3C1 ;P= 0.049 to 0.0007;
methods; fig. S12, common; table S7C). These
regulons are primarily active within Ex and INT
neuron populations (highest in Ex neurons) and
less so in glia, consistent with previous studies
of ASD susceptibility gene expression patterns
(36,53) (Fig. 6G and fig. S12). However, we
note that there were several TF-risk regulons(e.g., SOX5 ,SOX6 ,TCF7L2 ,PAX6 ,a n d SREBF2 )
differentially expressed in ASD ASTRO1, homeo-
static MG1, and OPCs, in addition to neurons
(Fig. 6G and fig. S12). ASD risk gene enrichment
has not been demonstrated before in glial cells.
These regulons comprised genes that were
down-regulated, which was the expected direc-
tion given the observed down-regulation of TF
d r i v e r s ,a n dw h i c hw o u l do c c u rs u b s e q u e n tt o
haploinsufficiency of a risk gene, which is pre-
dicted for most of these genes in ASD.
We also examined whether these regulons ’
target genes were also enriched for ASD sus-
ceptibility genes (SFARI tier 1, 2, or syndromic)
( f i g .S 1 3 A ) ,a sw e l la sg e n e sa s s o c i a t e dw i t hi n -
tellectual disability (ID) ( 58) and fragile X pro-
tein (FMRP) targets ( 59). Indeed, many regulons
driven by ASD TF susceptibility genes, or those
enriched for ASD-common variation, were al-
so enriched for ASD risk genes ( n= 19) and
FRMP targets ( n= 17), whereas only a few
were enriched for ID risk genes ( n=5 ;F i g .
6H) relative to other regulons. Moreover, net-
works similarly generated from published
single-cell transcriptome data in schizophrenia
(60) lacked enrichment for ASD genes (fig.
S13B). Taken together, these data provide a
critical starting point for understanding the
alterations in cellular and circuit mechanisms
driven by specific risk genes in the brains of
individuals with ASD.
Discussion
In this study, we performed a comprehensive
single-cell genomic assessment of the frontal
cortex in individuals with ASD, substantially
extending previous observations and pro-
viding important insights into ASD biology.
The depth and breadth of this single-cell
analysis, involving large numbers of individu-
als and cells profiled, solidifies the picture of
the major cortical cell types affected in ASD,
including alterations in cell type composition,
remodeling of cell stat es, and the identifica-
tion of cell type –specific transcriptional cas-
cades. We also provide a reliable, comprehensive
list of DEGs, which showed high correspon-
dence to orthogonal bulk and spatial tran-
scriptomic data and demonstrated parallel

Individuals with autism may manifest a
diverse array of coexisting conditions (includ-
ing epilepsy, attention deficient hyperactivity
disorder, schizophrenia, gastrointestinal con-
ditions, cerebral palsy, bipolar disorder, anxiety),
traits (including apraxia or speech difficul-
ties, social communication differences, sensory
sensitivities, learning differences, specialized
interests), and related behaviors (such as
repetitive movements or “stimulatory-seeking, ”
echolalia, and more) that make up their indi-
vidual characteristics, or “neurotype, ”of ASD
(34,36–40,67–69). Thus, it will require large
numbers of individual samples to elucidate
subgroups and to definitively match specificpatient traits, such as cognition or social be-
havior, to the observed molecular and cellular
changes observed here. We note that our
analysis included tissue from five individuals
with a monogenic form of ASD, (dup)15q11-13,
who, despite manifesting distinctive gene ex-
pression patterns, do share the major tran-
scriptional alterations and pathways observed
in idiopathic ASD at the bulk level ( 7), which
we demonstrate here at the single-cell level.
Notably, genes within the 15q duplication re-
gion show considerable ce ll-to-cell variability
in their expression changes, further demon-
strating the importance of understanding celltype –specific effects of genetic variation, espe-
cially in the context of major changes in gene
dosage.
Finally, recent work has demonstrated cortex-
wide transcriptional changes in the ASD brain
(14), including primary sensory regions, which
is consistent with the pre ferential involvement
of neurons responsible for intracortical and
interhemispheric connectivity that we demon-
strate here. These data provide a starting point
for developing mechanistic, molecular, and cel-
lular explanations for observations of changes
in both short- and long-range cortical connec-
tivity and cortical circuits in ASD ( 3,65,70,71).
A major challenge is now to understand how
these cell –cell interactions develop and evolve
at both a cellular and circuit level and to de-
termine how they relate to physiological and
behavioral states.
Materials and methods
Sample acquisition and preparation for
snRNA-seq and snATAC-seq
Postmortem cortical brain samples were ac-

formerly the Autism Tissue Project at Harvard
(ATP)] and the University of Maryland Brain
Banks (UMDB) through the NIH NeuroBioBank.
A total of 63 samples from subjects with ASD,
dup15q syndrome, and nonpsychiatric con-
trols from the prefrontal cortex (PFC) or from
Broadman area 9 (BA9) and to a smaller ex-
tent BA4/6. Thirty-one subjects had not beenpreviously profiled. Three samples were dropped
in the final integration. BA4/6 samples were pre-
viously subjected to bulk studies: Parikshak et al.,
Nature 2016 ( 7); Gandal et al.,Science 2018 ( 8),
and a small subset of samples (six samples) were
processed for a different single-cell analysis in
Gandal et al.,Nature 2022 ( 14).
Frozen brain samples were placed on dry ice
in a dehydrated dissection chamber to reduce
degradation effects from sample thawing and/or
humidity. Approximately 20 to 50 mg of cortex
was sectioned, ensuring specific gray matter –

After sequencing, Cell Ranger software from
10x Genomics ( https://support.10xgenomics.
com/single-cell-gene-expression/software ) was
used to prepare fastq files, and reads were
aligned to the human GRCh38 pre-mRNA ge-
nome to generate gene-by-cell matrices for each
library. Pegasus ( https://github.com/lilab-bcb/
pegasus ), a Python-based program, was used to

analysis with top 10 principal components (PCs)
and removed an identified low-quality cell clus-

mito_percent (m itochondrial gene percentage)
and low ngenes (number of genes per cell).
Then we reran the analysis with top 65 PCs after
removing these cells. Cells were filtered or re-
moved if they expressed >6000 or <250 genes
or if they had >10% mitochondrially mapped
reads. Dimensional reduction was done by prin-
cipal components analy sis (PCA) with n_genes
and percent_mito regressed out. Harmony (as
part of the Pegasus suite) was used to integrate
and batch-correct librar ies. Louvain clustering
was performed to cluster the cells and visual-
ize resulting clusters with uniform manifoldapproximation and projection (UMAP).
Cell type annotation
Cell types were annotated on the basis of ex-pression of known marker genes visualized by
UMAP and by performing unbiased gene
marker analysis (table S1C). Canonical genes
were selected on the basis of mouse and hu-
man studies as well as published reference
atlas enriched genes ( 15–18). We integrated
the Velmeshev et al. (13)d a t a s e tw i t ho u rc l u s -
ters through Seurat ’s R-based program ( 72)
(https://satijalab.org/seurat/index.html ), im-
plementation of FindTransferAnchors and
TransferData functions as detailed in vig-
nettes online ( https://satijalab.org/seurat/
articles/integration_mapping.html ). In brief,the functions aim to build cell pairwise cor-
respondences between single cells across the
reference datasets and query datasets using
PCA coordinates, thus allowing integration
of datasets into a shared space and serving
as an effective matching tool of one cluster
to another on a cell-by-cell basis. We also used
Azimuth, a web-based portal of the same
Seurat functions above, from the Allen Brain
Atlas ( 19)(https://azimuth.hubmapconsortium.
org) to align our cell clusters to the human
and mouse motor cortex clusters [BICCN ( 18)]
(table S1D).
Cortical cell composition analysis
A cell type –by-subject count matrix of cell num-
ber per subject per cluster was generated from
metadata. Data were then transformed to cell
proportions by total cells for each library and
log normalized. We then used the R-package
LimmaVoom ( 73) to stringently ask whether
any clusters were significantly over- or under-
represented (FDR ≤0.1) in the ASD subjects in
comparison to CTL subjects by implement-
ing a linear model (co-variables were included
if a Spearman correlation was >0.25 against
the top five clustering PCs): ~diagnosis +
Chemistry10X + age + PMI (post mortem in-
terval) + totalReads (table S3).

(UV) light –photocleavable oligo-probes of about
18,000 genes from the human genome. We as-
sisted the NanoString technician, J. Gong, with
choosing regions of interest (ROIs), and we
created three or four ROIs within gray matter
for L1/2, L2/3, L3/4, L5/6, and three ROIs within

Mapping gene activity signatures to layers
To look for spatial activity across the layer data-set using cell type annotation markers and/orASD DEGs, we first filtered each cell type –

representative list containing only positive

cell type –specific ASD DEGs, only significantly
down-regulated genes (FDR < 0.05 and logFC
> 0.2) were used to query layer activity for in-

effects and diagnosis and layer interaction ef-

using estimated marginal means (least-squares
means).

Common variation enrichment in regulons
Partitioned heritability of regulons and ASDcommon variants ( 37) was assessed using LD
Score Regression v1.0.0 ( 75). Heritability was
calculated by comparing the association statis-
tics for common genetic variants falling with-
in regulatory elements associated with specific
regulon genes, with the LD-score, a measure of
the extent of the LD block. First, an annota-
tion file was created, which marked all single-
nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) that fellwithin the regulatory elements for each regulon
gene (10 kb up- and downstream of gene). LD-
scores were calculated for these SNPs within
1-cM windows using the 1000 Genomes Euro-
pean (EUR) data. The enrichment coefficient
was calculated as the heritability explained for
ASD common variation within a given annota-
tion divided by the proportion of SNPs in the
genome and subjected to Bonferroni correction.

using TOBIAS ( 56), as described in our previous
study ( 57). Briefly, this method starts with Tn5
bias correction using the TOBIAS ATACorrect
module, subtracting the background Tn5 in-
sertion cuts highlighting the effect of protein
binding. The footprint score was calculated by
TOBIAS ScoreBigWig, which measures both
accessibility and depth of the local footprint,
thus correlating with the presence of a TF atits target loci, and the chromatin accessibility
of the regions where this TF binds. To match
footprints to potential TF binding sites and to
estimate TF binding activity on its target loci, we
applied TOBIAS BINDetect module to the cor-
rected ATACseq signals within peaks, with TF
motif position weight matrices from TRASFAC
Pro. To avoid motif redundancy, we clustered the
motifs according to their sequence similarity
using TOBIAS ClusterMotifs and chose one
motif per TF that is most similar to others in
the same cluster. TOBIAS BINDetect compares
the positions and activities of TF footprinted
sites in disease or control per cluster. Each foot-
print site was assigned a log2FC between two
conditions, representing whether the binding
site has larger or smaller TF footprint scores incomparison. To calculate statistics, a back-
ground distribution of footprint scores is built
by TOBIAS randomly subsetting peak regions
at ~200-bp intervals, and these scores were
used to calculate a distribution of background
log2FCs for each comparison of two condi-
tions. The global distribution of log2FCs per
TF was compared to the background distri-
butions to calculate a differential TF binding
score, which represents differential TF activ-
ity between two conditions. A Pvalue is cal-
c u l a t e db yT O B I A Sb ys u b s a m p l i n g1 0 0l o g 2 F C s
from the background and calculating the sig-
nificance of the observed change. By compar-ing the observed log2FC distribution to the
background log2FC, the effects of any global
differences due to sequencing depth, noise,
etc., are controlled. To visualize, we used soGGi
to plot TF footprints and bar graphs to show
the global TF footprint activity changes com-
paring ASD versus control.

INTRODUCTION: Historically, psychiatric disor-
ders have been distinguished from neurolog-
ical disorders by the ab sence of the associated
histological pathology observed in neurological
c o n d i t i o n s .B u t ,o v e rt h ep a s t1 5y e a r s ,e p i g e -netic and transcriptional profiling of postmor-
tem brain samples from multiple psychiatric
conditions, including autism spectrum dis-
order (ASD), have revealed robust underlying
molecular differences I nA S D ,t h i sr e f l e c t su p -
regulation of immune signaling genes, down-
regulation of neuronal markers and synaptic
genes, and a blunting of gene expression sig-natures of cortical regional identity How a
genetically complex condition such as ASD
converges on shared transcriptional altera-
tions remains a mystery This gap is further
amplified by the lack of biological insightsinto the differences in laminar and cell type –
specific pathways affected in ASD and the
underlying gene regulatory mechanisms.

level0_chunks.chunk_id: Molecular cascades and cell type–specific signatures in ASD revealed by single-cell genomics_rationale_0
level0_chunks.content:
RATIONALE: We reasoned that deep molecular
profiling at the single-cell level would inform
our understanding of changes in cortical cell
types and circuits and, when integrated withgenetic risk factors, enable identification of
candidate drivers of pathways altered in ASD Further, knowledge of these pathways at a cel-
lular level would inform mechanistically driven
therapeutic development RESULTS: We conducted single-nucleus RNA
sequencing (snRNA-seq) and single-nucleus as-
say for transposase-accessible chromatin with
sequencing (snATAC-seq) in a large ASD and
control (CTL) cohort, as a core component of
the PsychENCODE Cons ortium (https://www psychencode.org/), to identify cell type –specific
changes and the cellular regulatory networksperturbed by genetic risk factors Our ap-
proach (on average >10,000 cells per individual
and >1860 genes per cell) enabled identification
of all 26 major cortical cell types, validated with
published cortical cell atlases We also identified
cell states, primarily activated forms of mi-
croglia (MG), oligodendrocytes (ODCs), as-
trocytes (ASTROs), and blood-brain barrier
cells, observed predominantly in ASD Changes
in cell composition in ASD were subtle, involving
increases in activated mi croglia and astrocyte
states, which are very rarely observed in controls In contrast to the minor changes in cell
composition, the changes observed in gene
expression in ASD were substantial: 2166 down-
regulated and 1319 up-regulated genes across
35 cell types, most of which were cell type spe-
cific Through integration of snRNA-seq, snATAC-
seq, and spatial transcriptomics, we identified
regulatory networks driving cell type –specific
transcriptional changes and their location
within cortical laminae

transcriptional changes and their location
within cortical laminae These analyses dem-
onstrate concentration o f activated microglia,
astrocytes, and somatostatin (SST) interneurons
in superficial cortical laminae, in conjunction
with profound down-regulation of synaptic gene
expression and up-regulation of stress-response
and proinflammatory pathways in inter- and
intrahemispheric projection neurons A large
proportion of these changes could be ascribed to
specific transcriptional drivers, and both the driv-
ers and their targets were enriched in genes
harboring common and rare genetic risk for ASD.

Genomic profiling in postmortem brain from autistic individuals has consistently revealed convergent
molecular changes What drives these changes and how they relate to genetic susceptibility in this
complex condition are not well understood We perfor med deep single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq)
to examine cell composition and transcriptomi cs, identifying dysregulation of cell type –specific gene
regulatory networks (GRNs) in autism spectrum disord er (ASD), which we corrobora ted using sing le-nucleus
assay for transposase-accessible chromatin with sequ encing (snATAC-seq) and spatial transcriptomics Transcriptomic changes were primarily cell type specific, involving multiple cell types, most prominently
interhemispheric and callosal-projecting neurons, interneurons within superficial laminae, and distinct
glial reactive states involving oligodendrocytes, microglia, and astrocytes

level0_chunks.chunk_id: Molecular cascades and cell type–specific signatures in ASD revealed by single-cell genomics_conclusion_2
level0_chunks.content:
We perfor med deep single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq)
to examine cell composition and transcriptomi cs, identifying dysregulation of cell type –specific gene
regulatory networks (GRNs) in autism spectrum disord er (ASD), which we corrobora ted using sing le-nucleus
assay for transposase-accessible chromatin with sequ encing (snATAC-seq) and spatial transcriptomics Transcriptomic changes were primarily cell type specific, involving multiple cell types, most prominently
interhemispheric and callosal-projecting neurons, interneurons within superficial laminae, and distinct
glial reactive states involving oligodendrocytes, microglia, and astrocytes Autism-associated GRN
drivers and their targets were enriched in rare and common genetic risk variants, connecting autism
genetic susceptibility and cellular and circuit alterations in the human brain Psychiatric disorders are defined primar-
ily by behavioral and cognitive character-
istics and are classically distinguished
from neurological disorders by the ab-sence of the associated visible histo-
logical pathology observed in neurological
conditions However, a growing body of evi-
dence based on genomic profiling reveals con-
sistent molecular differences in brain tissue
from specific neuropsychiatric conditions com-
pared with brain tissue from neurotypical in-
dividuals ( 1–5) In autism spectrum disorder
(ASD), robust transcriptomic and epigenetic
alterations in the cerebral cortex have been
documented over the past decade, delineating
a reproducible pattern of molecular differences
(5–13) This robust molecular signature ob-
tained primarily from transcriptomic profiling
of bulk cortical tissue has identified convergent
biological pathways in the ASD brain, which is
characterized by an up-regulation of immune
signaling genes, down-regulation of specific
neuronal markers and synaptic genes, and an
attenuation of the typical patterns of gene ex-
pression associated with cortical regional iden-
tity (6–8,12–14)

level0_chunks.content:
In autism spectrum disorder
(ASD), robust transcriptomic and epigenetic
alterations in the cerebral cortex have been
documented over the past decade, delineating
a reproducible pattern of molecular differences
(5–13) This robust molecular signature ob-
tained primarily from transcriptomic profiling
of bulk cortical tissue has identified convergent
biological pathways in the ASD brain, which is
characterized by an up-regulation of immune
signaling genes, down-regulation of specific
neuronal markers and synaptic genes, and an
attenuation of the typical patterns of gene ex-
pression associated with cortical regional iden-
tity (6–8,12–14) These genomic data represent an essential
lens through which to understand the cellularand physiological changes occurring in the
brains of autistic individuals and to describe
potential causal mecha nisms through their in-
tegration with genetic risk variants ( 1,4,5) However, small sample sizes, in the case of
single-cell analysis ( 13), or profiling restricted
to bulk tissue have limited biological insights
as to the differences in laminar, circuit-level,
and cell type –specific pathways affected in
ASD, as well as their underlying gene regula-
tory mechanisms To address these limitations,
we leveraged advances in single-cell analyses to
profile the largest ASD cohort to date, consist-
ing of 63 cases and controls, including five cases
of a monogenic cause of ASD, 15q11-13 dupli-
cation [(dup)15q11-13] This resource, generated
as a core component of the PsychENCODE
Consortium ( 1,2,4,5,8), enabled our iden-
tification of the major cortical cell types af-
fected in the ASD cortex, including alterations
in glia cell composition and cell type –specific
transcriptional cascade s linking genes to func-
tion

To address these limitations,
we leveraged advances in single-cell analyses to
profile the largest ASD cohort to date, consist-
ing of 63 cases and controls, including five cases
of a monogenic cause of ASD, 15q11-13 dupli-
cation [(dup)15q11-13] This resource, generated
as a core component of the PsychENCODE
Consortium ( 1,2,4,5,8), enabled our iden-
tification of the major cortical cell types af-
fected in the ASD cortex, including alterations
in glia cell composition and cell type –specific
transcriptional cascade s linking genes to func-
tion Through integration of single-nucleus
RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq), single-nucleus
assay for transposase-ac cessible chromatin with
sequencing (snATAC-seq), and layer-specific spa-
tial transcriptomics, we describe and validate
regulatory networks driving cell type –specific
transcriptional changes and their location
within cortical laminae, providing a deeper
understanding of the biological mechanismsthat underlie ASD.

level0_chunks.content:
Results
Single-cell genomic analysis of human ASD
and control cortex
We generated snRNA-seq from the human
frontal cortex (Brodmann areas 9 and 4/6)from 33 ASD and 30 control subjects (Fig 1A
and table S1A), profiling, on average, >10,000
cells per individual (fig S1, A and B) We
included five individuals with a monogen-
ic form of ASD, 15q duplication syndrome
[(dup)15q11-13; table S1A], where transcrip-
tomic changes in bulk tissue mirror those ob-
served from cases of idiopathic ASD ( 7,8) Individual samples were taken from patients
ranging in age from 2 to 60 years (mean age:
20) and were selected to be matched by age, sex,
and cause of death balanced across cases and
controls (fig S1, B to D, and table S1A) We
isolated >800,000 nuclei and performed snRNA-
seq using the 10x Genomics platform (Materi-
als and methods) After quality control and
doublet removal, we analy zed high-quality tran-
scriptomes from 591,043 nuclei representing
306,347 cells from ASD subjects and 284,696
cells from control subje cts (average read depth
of 6.6 × 104per cell) with a mean of 1860 genes
and 4164 RNA molecules detected per cell (fig S1B), which provided an increase in power over
previous work ( 13) (table S1B) We simulta-
neously isolated nuclei to generate chroma-
tin conformation states using snATAC-seq in
22 cases and controls to validate predicted cell
type –specific regulatory networks through
identification of enrich ed transcription factor
(TF) binding sites with open chromatin and
TF footprinting analyses (Fig 1A) We performed unsupervised clustering of
transcriptional signatures from both ASD cases
and controls while considering biological and
technical sources of variation (methods) Visual-
ization of single-nuclei transcriptomes grouped
nuclei into 35 clusters that were not driven by
batch, Brodmann area, or individual samples
(Fig 1, B and C, and fig S1, A, C, and D)

annotated the clusters into seven major classes
of cortical cell types —neurons, specifically ex-
citatory neurons (Ex ne urons) and inhibitory
neurons (INTs); glial ce lls, including microglia
(MG), astrocytes (ASTRO), oligodendrocyte
progenitor cells (OPCs), and oligodendrocytes
(ODCs); and blood-brain barrier (BBB) cells —
on the basis of previousl y established cell type –

and mouse datasets ( 15–19), revealing the ex-

cortex ( 18) (Fig 1D and fig S1E) Next, we
annotated distinct subgroups within each
major class by aligning our cell clusters with
reference data from the Brain Initiative Cell

Brain Atlas ( 19), as well as a previous snRNA-
seq dataset from individuals with ASD and
controls ( 13) and using cluster-specific dif-
ferential marker genes (table S1C; methods) Each of our 35 clusters corresponded with the
cell profiles previously defined (Fig 1E and table

clusters identified in the previous, smaller ASD

1 Single-cell analysis of the ASD cortex (A) Schematic of the major
components of the study The frontal cortices (BA9/4/6) of the largest cohort of
ASD and CTL individuals were subjected to snRNA-seq, and one-third of these
samples were also subjected to snATAC-seq Samples were then analyzed for
changes in cell composition, and spatially resolved transcriptomics was
conducted to assess laminar-level changes in cell types and differential gene
expression We generated regulatory networks (SCENIC) that drive cell type –
specific changes in DEGs and validated these changes with TF footprinting
(TOBIAS) within open-chromatin changes (snATAC-seq) ( B) UMAP of cell
clusters defined by snRNA-seq ( C) Individual sample proportions of cell clusters
show even distribution across clusters ( D) Stacked violin plots of marker
gene expression in all clusters for OLIG1 for OPCs; MOG for ODCs (and OPCs);
GAD2 andANK1 for INTs; SLC17A7 andSATB2 for Ex neurons; EBF1 andDUSP1to mark pericytes, SM, and endothelial cells of the BBB; PTPRC for microglia; and
RFX4 andALDH1A1 for astrocytes Violin plots are split colored to mark CTL
expression in blue and ASD expression in red ( E) Sankey plot of cell cluster
equivalents from this current study (left) to reference cell types from BICCN
(18), human motor cortex (center), and Velmeshev et al.(13), human prefrontal
cortex (right) The height of the colored bar for each cell type depicts the
number of cells from this current study from the left to center; the height of bar
from the center to the right represents the number of cells from Velmeshev ( 13)
cluster types ( F) Significant increase in reactive astrocytes and microglia in
cortex from individuals with ASD Cell proportions for ASTRO1 (FDR = 0.10, P=
0.006, logFC = 0.3; left) and MG2 (FDR = 0.046, P= 0.001, logFC = 0.51; right),
from CTL individuals (black) and ASD individuals (red)

pathways in these cells included oxidative
phosphorylation and inflammatory stress re-
sponses (involving RPS16 ,CD47 ,DNAJB4 ,HSPA5 ,

TGF- b/epidermal growth factor (EGF)/mitogen-

(such as CAMK2A ,CAMKV ,EPHA4 ,a n d GAP43 )
(Fig 2B and table S4, A to C) In contrast to EXT_6
L23 neurons, EXT_4_L56 cortical-projecting
neurons manifested down-regulation of signal-
ing by NTRKs ( NTRK3 ,AKAP5 ,DLGAP2 ,a n d
SLIT2 ) and neurodevelopmental genes related
to axon guidance ( DAB1 ,ARC,SYNPO , and
TCF12 ; Fig 2C and table S4, A to C) These
neurons also exhibited up-regulation of genes
related to mRNA splicing ( HNRNPK ,SNRPC ,
andSLU7 ), ubiquitin protein ligand (such as
USPS ,UBE2K ,a n d CUL1 ), a stronger inflam-
matory response ( CD47 ,HLA-A ,IFI6,RPL10 ,
RPLP1 ,EEF1A2 , and DNAJB14 ), and intracel-
lular signaling involving proinflammatory
TGF- bsignals ( TGFB2 ,SEMA6A ,a n d SPP1 ;

These
neurons also exhibited up-regulation of genes
related to mRNA splicing ( HNRNPK ,SNRPC ,
andSLU7 ), ubiquitin protein ligand (such as
USPS ,UBE2K ,a n d CUL1 ), a stronger inflam-
matory response ( CD47 ,HLA-A ,IFI6,RPL10 ,
RPLP1 ,EEF1A2 , and DNAJB14 ), and intracel-
lular signaling involving proinflammatory
TGF- bsignals ( TGFB2 ,SEMA6A ,a n d SPP1 ;
Fig 2C and table S4, A to C) These data
provided evidence that these two classes of Ex
intercortical projection neurons exhibited the
largest degree of transcriptional dysregulation
relative to other neuronal classes (Fig 2A),
implicating disruption in long-range cortical
connectivity in ASD Both populations also
up-regulated genes annotated as proinflam-
matory Yet these two clusters of Ex projection
neurons in different cortical laminae displayed
distinct patterns of down-regulation in genes
composing biological pathways broadly related
to neuronal signaling and neurodevelopment We next compared the transcriptional changes
in both Ex cell types above to changes withinINTs showing the most DEGs, the SST+ INTs
(INT_5_SST) We observed a similar down-
regulation of pathways related to synaptic vesi-
cle regulation, neurotransmission, and synaptic
organization (fig S5A and table S4, A to C) However, INT_5_SST neurons showed a more
prominent down-regulation of genes directly
related to glutamatergic receptor function and
signaling (involving GRIA1/2/3 ,GRIN2A/3A ,
GRIN2B ,HOMER1 ,SHANK3 ,NLGN1 , and
TIAM1 ), structural and functional components
of the action potential (including SCN3B ,ANK2 ,
SCN1A ,SCN8A ,a n d SCN2A ), and mRNA splicing,
including members of the RBFOX and STAR
families (such as RBFOX1 ,SLM1 ,a n d SLM2
),
which play critical roles in synaptic connectivity
in these cells in mouse ( 42,43) (fig S5A andtable S4, A to C)

prominent down-regulation of genes directly
related to glutamatergic receptor function and
signaling (involving GRIA1/2/3 ,GRIN2A/3A ,
GRIN2B ,HOMER1 ,SHANK3 ,NLGN1 , and
TIAM1 ), structural and functional components
of the action potential (including SCN3B ,ANK2 ,
SCN1A ,SCN8A ,a n d SCN2A ), and mRNA splicing,
including members of the RBFOX and STAR
families (such as RBFOX1 ,SLM1 ,a n d SLM2
),
which play critical roles in synaptic connectivity
in these cells in mouse ( 42,43) (fig S5A andtable S4, A to C) The up-regulated genes in
SST+ INTs overlapped with several pathways
up-regulated in EXT_4_L56 cortical projection
neurons, including increases in inflammatory
response ( HLA-A ,B2M,a n d IGF1R )a n dp r o t e i n
modification, as well as an increase in transport
along cytoskeleton and calcium-mediated axon
guidance related genes ( RAC1 ,RDX,SCNA ,a n d
MAPT ; fig S5A and table S4, A to C) Mapping
the SST+ INT cluster –specific down-regulated
DEGs onto the spatial transcriptomic dataset
demonstrated that this DEG signature was
most significantly altered within superficial
layers in the ASD cortex, suggesting that SST+INTs in these laminae were the most affected
(fig S5A; right panel, P=0  0 0 7i nL 2 / 3 ,l i n e a r
mixed model; methods) Glial changes
Glial cells in ASD were primarily characterizedby changes in the state of these cells from a
homeostatic, or resting, state to reactive or ac-
tivated inflammatory states, compared with
controls This change was illustrated by up-
regulation of cell type –specific responses to
inflammatory and interferon signaling and a
parallel decrease in expression of homeostatic
genes ( 21,26) We describe in the following
paragraphs the ASD reactive inflammatory
states in the major glial types: astrocytes, mi-
croglia, and ODCs

level0_chunks.content:
This change was illustrated by up-
regulation of cell type –specific responses to
inflammatory and interferon signaling and a
parallel decrease in expression of homeostatic
genes ( 21,26) We describe in the following
paragraphs the ASD reactive inflammatory
states in the major glial types: astrocytes, mi-
croglia, and ODCs Genes up-regulated in protoplasmic (PP) gray
matter astrocytes (ASTRO1) represent astrocyte
proliferation (including FOXO3 ,RFX7 , and
ZEB1 ) and likely lie downstream of TGF- band
interferon signaling through major histocom-
patibility complex (MHC) , other neural-immune
receptors (including HLA-B ,HLA-C ,HLA-E ,
CD44 ,IFI6,IFITM2 ,IFGR1 ,TGFBR2 , and
BMP7 ), and their inflammatory response effec-
tors (including IRF1,JAK3 ,MED12L ,SMARCA2 ,
STAT1/3 ,a n d SMAD1/3 ;F i g .3 Aa n dt a b l eS 4 A )
(44,45), which are up-regulated in parallel Fibrous (FB) astrocytes (ASTRO3) exhibited
similar changes, such as up-regulation of MHC
and other receptors (including HLA-B ,HLA-C ,
HLA-E ,CD99 ,CD44 ,a n d NTRK2 ), but differed
by up-regulation of cytoskeleton morphogene-
sis and focal adhesion signaling (genes includ-
ingITGB5 ,ITGAV ,TAB2 ,KALRN ,a n d NAV3 ),
suggesting changes in morphology or projec-
tions from white matter FB astrocytes in the ASD
cortex FB astrocytes (ASTRO3) also up-regulated
genes related to stress-related apoptosis and un-
folded protein response (involving
DNAJA4 ,
HSP90AA1 ,HSPA1B ,BAG3 ,a n d DAB2IP )( F i g  3B and table S4A) Both PP and FB astrocytes
exhibited a down-regulation of lipid and cho-
lesterol biosynthesis pathway genes ( HMGCS1 ) However, PP astrocytes had down-regulated
growth factor and NTRK signaling genes, where-
as the opposite was true for FB astrocytes in ASD
relative to controls Spe cifically, FB astrocytes
up-regulated expression of TGF- bsignaling(TGFB1 ), growth factors ( VEGFA ), and extra-
cellular matrix proteins (including ADAM12
andADAMTS17 ) (Fig 3B and table S4A)

level0_chunks.chunk_id: Molecular cascades and cell type–specific signatures in ASD revealed by single-cell genomics_results_20
level0_chunks.content:
Spe cifically, FB astrocytes
up-regulated expression of TGF- bsignaling(TGFB1 ), growth factors ( VEGFA ), and extra-
cellular matrix proteins (including ADAM12
andADAMTS17 ) (Fig 3B and table S4A) Microglia (MG2) manifested an increase in
reactive-state markers, as highlighted by the
up-regulation of known prophagocytotic genes
(such as P2RX7 ,TLR1/2/5 ,a n d CD68 ), includ-
ing pronounced up-regulation of the extra-
cellular signaling molecule, SPP1 ( 46)( F i g .3 C )  MG2 cells also expressed a higher number of
MHC I and II class molecules, complement,
and receptors (involving HLA-A/B/C ,FCGR1A/
1B/3A ,C1QC ,C1QA ,TNR,a n d TGFBR1 ), more
so than the other glial cell classes In ASD,reactive MG2 cells also increased expression
of genes related to cell morphogenesis (includ-
ingCAMKV ,TAOK1/3 ,CTNNB1 ,MAPK10/14 ,
andJAK2/3 ) and integrin signaling (including
CD68 ,CD86 ,ITGB1 ,ITGAX ,ITGAV ,a n d ITGA9 ),
which suggests an increase in migration and
formation of contacts with other cells (Fig 3C
and table S4A) Since many of these changes
are thought to be downstream of cytokine sig-
naling, we hypothesize from these data that
SPP1 may be acting as an extracellular element
responsible for coor dinating the cell –cell inter-
actions putatively directing synaptic and/or
cellular removal in activated MG (
46,47) We also observed that ODCs have shifted
from a homeostatic state to a more immuno-
reactive state in ASD, another glial change
that has not previously been recognized For
example, oligodendrocytes in cluster ODC1
up-regulated genes related to inflammatory
and energy stress response (involving IFIT1 ,
BAG3 ,ABAT ,EARS2 ,NMNAT3 ,EIF4A1 , and
EIF3A ) and histone modifying enzymes (in-
volving HDAC4/5/7 ,KDM5A ,EP300 ,a n dKMT2A )
(Fig 3D and table S4A) However, ODC1 also
contained a substantial number of down-
regulated genes, the largest of any glia cell
type and similar in magnitude to that of super-
ficial L23 Ex neurons (Fig 2B)

level0_chunks.content:
However, ODC1 also
contained a substantial number of down-
regulated genes, the largest of any glia cell
type and similar in magnitude to that of super-
ficial L23 Ex neurons (Fig 2B) Enriched down-
regulated pathways included cadherin signaling
(including CTNNB1/2 ,GSK3B ,FZD3 ,a n d CDH2/
8/11/19/20 ), transport along microtubule (in-
cluding KIF3A andDOCK9/10/3/5 ), and mye-
lination (including MBP ,PLP1 ,MAG ,JAM3 ,
LGI4 ,a n d MYRF ), which predict a potential
reduction in the capability of ODC1 cells to ma-
ture and functionally extend their processes,
adhere, and properly myelinate neuronal axons
(Fig 3D and table S4A) Defining the regulatory networks underlying
transcriptional changes
We next systematically integrated the cell type –
specific ASD DEG data with TF networks to
discover candidate drivers of the observed cell
type –specific transcriptional changes in ASD
relative to controls and to determine whether
these could be related to causal genetic fac-
tors (Fig 4A) We first analyzed the single-
cell transcriptomes with SCENIC ( 48,49),DECODING THE BRAIN

regulons, consist of the TF and its downstream
target genes [which are significantly coexpressed
by FDR < 0.05 and harbor the TF motif within
10 kb of the transcription start site (TSS)] We first scored each regulon across cells to
identify which regulons were preferentially
associated with ASD, and then we determinedthe extent of overlap of each regulon with cell
type –specific DEGs (Fig 4A; methods) We found that 217 of 337 regulons detected
were predicted to be altered in ASD in at least

ized the top ASD regulons predicted to regulate
the most DEGs by cell type: L23 Ex neurons,
SST+ INTs, and MG2 (Fig 4, B to D ; fig S6;
and table S5, C to E; methods)

TheCUX1 down-regulated regulons within
both neuronal types formed direct protein –
protein interaction (PPI) networks, which were
also significantly enriched for ASD-associated
risk genes (OR = 3, P=1×1 0−46,a n dO R=
2.5,P=1×1 0−20; hypergeometric tests), includ-

drivers ( TAF1 ,SREBF2 ,KDM5A ,a n d BCL11A ;
Fig 5, A and B; methods) The CUX1 regulon
within EXT_6_L23 was composed of genes
that function within the Golgi apparatus and
nucleus, related to catalytic activity on a pro-
tein (including SYNJ2 ,MTOR ,CYTH1 ,PSEN1 ,
PLCB4 ,IQSEC2 ,ERBB4 ,SFPQ ,a n d HIP1)a n d
gene expression (including EP300 ,MED27 ,SMAD3 ,SREBF2 ,NPAS2 ,NCOA3 ,a n d NCOR2 ;
Fig 5, A and C) The CUX1 regulon set of down-
regulated genes within SST+ INTs was enriched
for genes that function in synaptic signal-
ing, such as calcium and potassium voltage-
gated ion channels (involving CACNA1B ,
CACNA1A ,KCNQ3 ,CACNA1D ,KCNC2 ,a n d
CACNA1C ) and guanosine triphosphatase
activity (involving TIAM1 ,RASGRF2 ,FAM49B ,
KALRN ,AUTS2 ,a n d STMN 1; Fig 5, B and D) The spatial distributions of down-regulated
genes from the L23 Ex neuron and SST+ INT
regulons indicated that these networks were
most reduced in layers 2 and 3 in ASD (Fig 5,

Regulatory networks driving cell type –specific transcriptional
changes (A) Schematic of network discovery using SCENIC Initial coexpression
networks were generated from cellular transcriptional profiles and then pruned to
TF-driven regulatory networks, called regulons, consisting of the TF and its
downstream target genes (that were significantly, FDR < 0.05, coexpressed and
harbor the TF motif within 10 kb of TSS); regulons were then scored to identify
which were changed within ASD, followed by assessing their overlap with
cell type –specific DEGs ( B) Percent overlap between EXT_6_L23 down-regulatedDEGs and regulons predicted to regulate DEGs [highest percentage overlap
(blue) to lowest percentage overlap (yellow)] These regulons together account
for 64% of down-regulated DEGs in EXT_6_L23 ( C) Overlap of INT_5_SST
down-regulated DEGs and largest regulons predicted to regulate DEGs (blue to
yellow) Together they account for 54% of down-regulated DEGs in SST+
INTs ( D) Percentage overlap between MG2 up-regulated DEGs and largest
regulons (red to yellow) Together they account for 47% of up-regulated genes
in MG2 cells *0.01 < P< 0.05; **0.001 < P< 0.01; *** P< 0.001.DECODING THE BRAIN

ses, which permitted testing of >130 TFs to

regulatory networks and experimental RNA-

leveraged a published Perturb-seq dataset in
K562 cells to test 10 overlapping TFs from
both datasets [( 52); methods], which also con-
firmed that their knockouts resulted in signif-
icant changes in the predicted regulon target
genes ( P=1  4 5×1 0−6permutation, see meth-
ods; fig S8C) These findings support our
regulon network relationships between TFs

Although SCENIC predictions have been shown
to be reliable in predicti ng experimentally val-
idated regulatory networks ( 1,53–55)a n d ,m o r e -
over, were supported by the in vitro experimental
perturbation data above, we next sought to
further validate regulatory changes of TFs We
investigated chromatin accessibility by per-
forming snATAC-seq from a subset of the same
22 samples (12 cases and 10 controls) subjected
to scRNA-seq (methods; table S6A) We gen-
erated >100,000 single-nucleus profiles after
quality control filtering, which we integrated
with the snRNA-seq to verify and validate cell
type cluster annotations (Fig 6A and fig S9, A
and B; methods) We observed a high concor-
dance between the snATAC-seq and snRNA-
seq clusters, as evidenced by high correlations
between cluster expression profiles (table S6B;
methods) Moreover, we assessed the overlapbetween snATAC-seq differential chromatin
accessibility and snRNA-seq –derived gene ex-
pression changes when there were sufficient
numbers of cells and gene expression changes
for adequate power, finding significant overlap
for most cell types as expected (figs S10, A to E,
and S11, A to E; Prange = 1.1 × 10−210to 0.04,
hypergeometric test) We next leveraged the open chromatin pro-
files from each major cell type to assess changes
in TF binding on the basis of DNA footprinting
using TOBIAS ( 56,57) (Fig 6B; methods) DNA
footprints overlapping with TF motifs were
defined as direct TF binding sites TF bindingactivities were then quantified by scoring each
footprint ’s depleted signal at its predicted
binding site relative to the surrounding back-
ground chromatin accessibility (methods)

defined as direct TF binding sites TF bindingactivities were then quantified by scoring each
footprint ’s depleted signal at its predicted
binding site relative to the surrounding back-
ground chromatin accessibility (methods) Using
this approach allowed us to more accurately
recover the binding activities of hundreds of
TFs at a time in comparison to other technol-
o g i e st h a tp e r m i ta s s e s s m e n to ft h ea c t i v i t yo f
one TF at a time ( 56) We focused on TFs pre-
dicted to account for the major changes in
DEGs described above (Figs 2 to 4 and fig S6) Within Ex L23 neurons, we observed that 48%
of the transcriptionally down-regulated TFs
predicted to drive downstream DEGs within
the network in ASD have changes in binding
occupancy within the relevant TF DNA foot-
prints (table S7A) For example, in EXT_6_L23
neurons, we saw a decrease in the footprint
activity of BCL6 (P=2  4 5×1 0
−114),TCF3 (P=
1.28 × 10−63), and MAFB (P=9  1 2×1 0−100)a s
well as an increase in binding for up-regulated
TFs such as FOSB (P=1  4 0×1 0−195),JDP2 (P=
1.24 × 10−196), and SMAD5 (P=4  1 6×1 0−128;
Fig 6C) with examples of altered footprints
forMEIS3 andELK1 (Fig 6D, footprints, and
table S7A) Likewise, within reactive MG2, we
validated the changes in target binding for
43% of transcriptionally altered TFs by foot-
printing (table S7B) We observed increases in
TF activity for IRF7 (P=2  3 5×1 0−132)a n d
POU2F2 (P=5  3 7×1 0−107)( F i g .6 Ea n dt a b l e
S7B) with examples of altered footprints for
JUND andNFKB1 (Fig 6F) in MG2 Altogether,
we found that the SCENIC regulatory net-
works and DEGs were mostly supported by TF
occupancy changes within open chromatin in
ASD relative to controls, which, when com-
bined with the perturbation experiments (fig S8), provide strong orthogonal experimental
support for regulon activity changes in ASD

we found that the SCENIC regulatory net-
works and DEGs were mostly supported by TF
occupancy changes within open chromatin in

support for regulon activity changes in ASD ASD risk gene enrichment
To determine whether these regulons repre-sent known causal aspects of ASD biology, we
next tested whether the drivers or their down-
stream gene targets were enriched in known
ASD risk genes (SFARI syndromic, tiers 1 and
2; methods) Indeed, 30 of the regulons dys-
regulated in ASD brain were driven by high-
confidence TF risk genes from the SFARIdatabase, a significant enrichment (including
CUX1 ,CHD2 ,FOXP1 ,BCL11A ,a n d SOX5 ;f i g  S12, rare, OR = 1.64, P= 0.004, hypergeometric
test) Further, 21 of these regulons were en-
riched for genes harboring common genetic
susceptibility for ASD ( 37) (including CELF4 ,
SREBF2 ,ETV5 ,a n d NR3C1 ;P= 0.049 to 0.0007;
methods; fig S12, common; table S7C) These
regulons are primarily active within Ex and INT
neuron populations (highest in Ex neurons) and
less so in glia, consistent with previous studies
of ASD susceptibility gene expression patterns
(36,53) (Fig 6G and fig S12) However, we
note that there were several TF-risk regulons(e.g., SOX5 ,SOX6 ,TCF7L2 ,PAX6 ,a n d SREBF2 )
differentially expressed in ASD ASTRO1, homeo-
static MG1, and OPCs, in addition to neurons
(Fig 6G and fig S12) ASD risk gene enrichment
has not been demonstrated before in glial cells These regulons comprised genes that were
down-regulated, which was the expected direc-
tion given the observed down-regulation of TF
d r i v e r s ,a n dw h i c hw o u l do c c u rs u b s e q u e n tt o

dicted for most of these genes in ASD

ASD risk gene enrichment
has not been demonstrated before in glial cells These regulons comprised genes that were
down-regulated, which was the expected direc-
tion given the observed down-regulation of TF
d r i v e r s ,a n dw h i c hw o u l do c c u rs u b s e q u e n tt o
haploinsufficiency of a risk gene, which is pre-
dicted for most of these genes in ASD We also examined whether these regulons ’
target genes were also enriched for ASD sus-
ceptibility genes (SFARI tier 1, 2, or syndromic)
( f i g .S 1 3 A ) ,a sw e l la sg e n e sa s s o c i a t e dw i t hi n -
tellectual disability (ID) ( 58) and fragile X pro-
tein (FMRP) targets ( 59) Indeed, many regulons
driven by ASD TF susceptibility genes, or those
enriched for ASD-common variation, were al-
so enriched for ASD risk genes ( n= 19) and
FRMP targets ( n= 17), whereas only a few
were enriched for ID risk genes ( n=5 ;F i g  6H) relative to other regulons Moreover, net-
works similarly generated from published
single-cell transcriptome data in schizophrenia
(60) lacked enrichment for ASD genes (fig S13B) Taken together, these data provide a
critical starting point for understanding the
alterations in cellular and circuit mechanisms
driven by specific risk genes in the brains of
individuals with ASD Discussion
In this study, we performed a comprehensive
single-cell genomic assessment of the frontal
cortex in individuals with ASD, substantially
extending previous observations and pro-
viding important insights into ASD biology The depth and breadth of this single-cell

tegration of snRNA-seq, snATAC-seq, and layer-
specific spatial transcr iptomics allowed us to
describe and validate candidate regulatory
networks driving cell type –specific transcrip-
tional changes and thei r location within cor-
tical laminae Although we observed broad
transcriptional changes in both inhibitory and
excitatory neurons, consistent with previous
observations in bulk tissue, the magnitude of
changes varied considerably by cell type We
found that most changes in neuronal gene
expression occur in glutamatergic neurons
within the superficial layers of the cortex, con-firming a previous, sma ller analysis implicat-
ing superficial-layer projection neurons ( 13) We also identified large changes in SST in-
terneurons, and intracortical projecting L56
neurons Moreover, these changes in neuronal
gene expression in ASD were accompanied by
marked shifts to more activated proinflamma-
tory states in multiple glial cell types, includ-
ing ODCs, MG, astrocytes, and cells that make
up the BBB These data are available to explore
as a resource on the PsychENCODE website
(61) and our ASD single-cell browser, the ASD
Single-Cell Gene Expression (scGENE) Portal
(http://solo.bmap.ucla.edu/asdscgene/ ) Transcriptomic changes associated with a
neuropsychiatric condition, although represent-
ing a quantitative genome-wide molecular mea-
surement, may represent the consequence of
that condition and do not necessarily imply

These data are available to explore
as a resource on the PsychENCODE website
(61) and our ASD single-cell browser, the ASD
Single-Cell Gene Expression (scGENE) Portal
(http://solo.bmap.ucla.edu/asdscgene/ ) Transcriptomic changes associated with a
neuropsychiatric condition, although represent-
ing a quantitative genome-wide molecular mea-
surement, may represent the consequence of
that condition and do not necessarily imply
causality We reasoned that by identifying po-
tential transcriptional regulators and sub-
sequently testing whether these TFs or their
downstream targets were enriched in genetic
risk, we could implicate potential causal driv-
ers Our analysis identified candidate TF driv-
ers that account for a substantial portion of
major gene expression changes in multiple
neuronal and glial cell types, of which many
were validated by the CMAP LINCS resource
a n dT Ff o o t p r i n t i n g .T h e s eT F s ,c o u p l e dw i t h
their downstream targets, called regulons, are
enriched in known high-confidence ASD risk
genes harboring rare variants and commonpolygenic risk score for ASD, which supports
their potential causal role in ASD pathoge-
nesis Moreover, these analyses delineate the
potential downstream consequences of these
causal genetic variants in the ASD brain by
identifying DEGs and the biological pathways
that are regulated by these risk genes in the
human brain These regulon networks asso-
ciated with ASD risk reflect down-regulation
of synaptic vesicle regul ation, neurotransmis-
sion, and components related to synaptic de-
velopment and organization pathways, which
have been observed in other studies ( 8,13,14) A number of these TFs have important roles
in the development and maintenance of cell
identity (e.g., CUX1 ,SOX6 ,a n d FOXP2 ), provid-
ing a link between fetal development, involv-ing ASD risk-locus enrichment in specific TFs,
and its postnatal ramifications, represented by
cortical transcriptional changes in ASD

level0_chunks.content:
These regulon networks asso-
ciated with ASD risk reflect down-regulation
of synaptic vesicle regul ation, neurotransmis-
sion, and components related to synaptic de-
velopment and organization pathways, which
have been observed in other studies ( 8,13,14) A number of these TFs have important roles
in the development and maintenance of cell
identity (e.g., CUX1 ,SOX6 ,a n d FOXP2 ), provid-
ing a link between fetal development, involv-ing ASD risk-locus enrichment in specific TFs,
and its postnatal ramifications, represented by
cortical transcriptional changes in ASD We
emphasize that more definitive determina-
tion of the causal impact of risk genes on these
transcriptional regulatory circuits awaits direct
experimental perturbations, for example, in hu-
m a ni nv i t r oo r g a n o i dm o d e l s( 62–64) These data support previous predictions of
ASD risk gene enrichment in superficial-layerneurons from developing neurotypical human
cortex ( 3,65) and extend these observations
by (i) implicating superficial SST+ INTs and
deep-layer, interhemispherically projectingEx neurons; (ii) linking regulatory networks
driven by ASD risk TFs to cell type –specific
DEGs in postnatal brain in ASD and apply-
ing spatial transcriptomics to corroborate the
laminar distribution of these changes; (iii) sug-
gesting that the shift in expression of homeo-
static genes to genes that underlie “reactive ”
or“activated inflammatory ”state in microglia
and astrocytes is enriched in superficial gray
matter layers and also extends to ODCs and
cells that make up the BBB; and (iv) showing
that some of these changes in microglia and
ODCs are linked to multiple candidate TF driv-
ers that are known ASD risk genes, providing a
potentially causal link to some of the reactive
changes in these glial cells Further, these data
support a mechanistic model for the potential
downstream impact of ASD risk genes through
their activity as transcriptional drivers These
TFs converge primarily in intracortical Ex pro-
jection neurons

level0_chunks.content:
Further, these data
support a mechanistic model for the potential
downstream impact of ASD risk genes through
their activity as transcriptional drivers These
TFs converge primarily in intracortical Ex pro-
jection neurons We posit that primary Ex
neuron dysfunction in conjunction with local
circuit interneurons may subsequently influ-
ence microglia and astr o c y t er e a c t i v es t a t e s ,
b e c a u s et h el a t t e ra r ea l s om o r ec o n c e n t r a t e d
in superficial cortical laminae, where both
risk genes and transcriptional changes are
most prominent These data are consistent
with the framing of ASD as a developmental
synaptic disconnection syndrome involving
intracortical connectivity ( 66)b u ta l s oi n d i c a t e
consequential local, presumably maladaptive,
changes in both inter neurons and glia that
could be leveraged as potential therapeutic
modulators Individuals with autism may manifest a
diverse array of coexisting conditions (includ-
ing epilepsy, attention deficient hyperactivity
disorder, schizophrenia, gastrointestinal con-
ditions, cerebral palsy, bipolar disorder, anxiety),
traits (including apraxia or speech difficul-
ties, social communication differences, sensory
sensitivities, learning differences, specialized
interests), and related behaviors (such as
repetitive movements or “stimulatory-seeking, ”
echolalia, and more) that make up their indi-
vidual characteristics, or “neurotype, ”of ASD
(34,36–40,67–69) Thus, it will require large
numbers of individual samples to elucidate
subgroups and to definitively match specificpatient traits, such as cognition or social be-
havior, to the observed molecular and cellular
changes observed here We note that our
analysis included tissue from five individuals
with a monogenic form of ASD, (dup)15q11-13,
who, despite manifesting distinctive gene ex-
pression patterns, do share the major tran-
scriptional alterations and pathways observed
in idiopathic ASD at the bulk level ( 7), which
we demonstrate here at the single-cell level
